title: To the Point
core: Every word here says a thing fits the matter at hand — but they split into two jobs that the exam keeps confusing. The first job is **admissibility**: does this belong in the discussion at all? That's a gatekeeper's ruling, and it says nothing about whether the remark was any good. The second job is **craft**: granting that it belongs, how well was it chosen — for precision, for timing, for pleasure? A dull, clumsy remark can pass the first test; a dazzling one can fail it.

words.nuance: The structural test: does this actually attach to *this* question? **Germane** is nearly binary and nearly always contested — you meet it negated, in the mouth of whoever is trying to shut a line of argument down. It grants nothing about quality or importance; a germane point can be trivial and badly made, it just isn't out of order.

Adds worth to attachment. Where *germane* asks "does it connect," **pertinent** rules that it connects hard enough to deserve the room's time — a verdict from someone with standing to make it (chair, judge, examiner). "Not pertinent" is dismissal by weight; "not germane" is dismissal by scope.

Drops admissibility entirely and praises **aim**. It attaches to things *said* — a quotation, an analogy, an example — and means the remark landed on the precise nerve of the matter, not merely near it. The bookish verdict of a critic; you cannot call a policy or a person apposite.

Praises the **moment**, not the content. An apposite remark stays apposite whenever you make it; an **apropos** one owes its force to arriving exactly then. It is also the only member with a prepositional life — *apropos of your last point* — and it keeps an urbane French air that reads as cultivated aloud, mannered on the page.

The plain-clothes member: neutral register, no ceremony, and the only one carrying senses that have nothing to do with relevance — *apt to overreact* (inclined), *an apt pupil* (quick to learn). Even in its fit sense it merely certifies accuracy; it neither delights like *felicitous* nor claims the surgical strike of *apposite*.

Fit **plus pleasure** — the listener feels a small click of rightness, which none of the others promises. Reserved for phrasing, titles, metaphors, and timing, and it is the only one whose negative is in live circulation: *infelicitous* is how a reviewer calls a line clumsy without saying so.

exam_note: Two traps: **apt** usually appears in its *tendency* sense (a near-synonym of *prone*, minus the disapproval), and blanks demanding relevance-as-admissibility (germane, pertinent) will offer craft words (apposite, felicitous) that praise the wrong thing.
